interactive.title: The stretch finder
interactive.whatAmILookingAt: This lesson runs over thirteen small screens. Each one shows the stretch finder. A probe arrow v, one unit long, starts at the origin. You drag its tip round the circle. A second arrow, Av, is drawn from the origin in a heavier line. It is v's first number times column 1, plus its second number times column 2. A ring traces where Av's tip goes as v goes round. Most of the time Av points away from v's line. When Av lies along v's line, that whole line lights. Near a lit line, v snaps onto it. A readout then gives λ, Av's length over v's length. λ carries a minus sign when Av points the opposite way. A matrix card shows the matrix. You change it by dragging where (1, 0) and (0, 1) land. Or you tap a preset: stretch [3 1; 0 2], mirror [0 1; 1 0], shear [1 1; 0 1] or quarter turn [0 −1; 1 0]. A λ slider runs from −2 to 6 in halves. It draws the grid of A − λI. That is A with λ taken off each diagonal entry. A readout gives its determinant, the area scale. At an eigenvalue the grid lies flat on one line, and the determinant reads 0. The line it crushes is drawn dashed. It is the lit line. Screen 1 shows A = [3 1; 0 2]. v starts at (0, 1). Av = (1, 2) points off its line. Then v sweeps round. At (1, 0), Av = (3, 0). The line lights and λ reads 3. Along (−1, 1), Av is twice v, and λ reads 2. The finished picture shows v on the line through (−1, 1), lit, with λ = 2. Screen 2 is a puzzle. For the same A, which arrow stays on its own line? The choices are (−2, 2), (1, 1) and (0, 1). The right answer is (−2, 2). It sits on the line already lit. Screen 3 shows the mirror [0 1; 1 0]. It swaps an arrow's two numbers. Along (1, 1), Av = v, and λ reads 1. Along (1, −1), Av points the opposite way on the same line. There λ reads −1. The finished picture shows v on the line through (1, −1), lit, with λ = −1. Screen 4 is a puzzle. Which keeps no line at all: the shear, the quarter turn or the mirror? You can tap each preset and sweep it to check. The quarter turn is right. The shear lights once, along (1, 0). Screen 5 shows A = [3 1; 0 2] again. Av = λv is written (A − λI)v = 0. So det(A − λI) = 0, the characteristic equation. The λ slider moves up from 0. The grid of A − λI shrinks. At λ = 2 it lies flat on one line, with determinant (3 − 2)(2 − 2) = 0. The dashed line is the line through (−1, 1), lit as before. At λ = 3 it goes flat again. This time it crushes the line through (1, 0). The finished picture shows λ = 2, flat. Screen 6 is a puzzle. Why write (A − λI)v = 0 and not (A − λ)v = 0? One choice says a matrix minus a number means nothing. One says λI keeps λ a whole number. One says I stops v being zero. Screen 7 shows B = [2 −1; −1 2]. Its trace is 4 and its determinant 3. So λ² − 4λ + 3 = 0, which is (λ − 1)(λ − 3) = 0. The grid goes flat at λ = 1 and at λ = 3. The finished picture shows λ = 3, flat. The line through (1, −1) is dashed and lit. Screen 8 is a puzzle. [4 1; 2 3] has one eigenvalue 5. What is the other? The choices are 2, 7 and −5. The right answer, 2, lights the line through (1, −2). 5 lights the line through (1, 1). Screen 9 goes back to B. The arrow v along (1, 1) is drawn from the start. For λ = 1, B − I = [1 −1; −1 1]. Both rows say v₁ − v₂ = 0. So v = (1, 1), or any multiple. For λ = 3, B − 3I = [−1 −1; −1 −1]. Both rows say v₁ + v₂ = 0, so v = (1, −1). The finished picture shows both lines lit. (1, 1) is labelled 1 and (1, −1) is labelled 3. Screen 10 is a puzzle. Take A = [3 1; 0 2] and λ = 3. Someone's working ends at v = (0, 0). What does that tell them? One choice says there is a slip in the working. One says (0, 0) is the eigenvector. One says 3 is not an eigenvalue. The first is right. A − 3I = [0 1; 0 −1] crushes the whole line through (1, 0). Screen 11 shows a 3-D view of C = [1 1 0; 1 2 1; 0 1 1]. You turn it by dragging the background. Expanding det(C − λI) gives −λ³ + 4λ² − 3λ = 0. It has no plain number term, so λ = 0 is a root. The rest is λ² − 4λ + 3 = 0. Three lines light: (1, −1, 1) with 0, (1, 0, −1) with 1 and (1, 2, 1) with 3. The line for 0 is also dashed, because it is C's null space. The finished picture shows all three lines lit. Screen 12 is a mixed puzzle. What are the eigenvalues of [5 2; 2 2]? The choices are 1 and 6, 5 and 2, or 3 and 4. Screen 13 is a mixed puzzle. [5 2; 2 2] has eigenvalues 1 and 6. Which pairing is right? The first choice is 6 with (2, 1) and 1 with (1, −2). The second is 6 with (1, −2) and 1 with (2, 1). The third is 6 with (2, 1) and 1 with (0, 0). The right answer lights both lines with their λ. Some screens show an idea. The rest ask you to try it. Each puzzle offers three answers. On a narrow phone they wrap onto more lines.
interactive.ignores: The probe snaps onto a lit line when it comes within 3° of it. That lets you find each line by hand. The lines themselves can point at any angle. The panel has edges, but each lit line goes on for ever in both directions. The quarter turn's eigenvalues are complex numbers, and so are its eigenvectors. A flat picture cannot draw them. The 3-D screen is a flat drawing too. Turning it helps you judge depth.

explain.text:
A matrix usually knocks an arrow off its own line. Along a few directions it only stretches or squishes the arrow. An arrow along one of these comes out as a number times itself: Av = λv. That arrow is an [[eigenvector]]. The number λ is its [[eigenvalue]], the factor it is stretched or squished by.[^1] You find the numbers first, from det(A − λI) = 0. Then you find each direction, from (A − λI)v = 0.

Take A = [3 1; 0 2]. Remember that Av is v's first number times column 1, plus its second number times column 2. The arrow (0, 1) gives column 2, which is (1, 2). That points somewhere else, so (0, 1) is knocked off its line. The arrow (1, 0) gives column 1, which is (3, 0). That is 3 lots of (1, 0), so λ = 3. The arrow (−1, 1) gives −(3, 0) + (1, 2) = (−2, 2). That is 2 lots of (−1, 1), so λ = 2. Each eigenvector is really a whole line of them, because any multiple works too. That whole line is the [[eigenspace]] for λ = 2. A(−2, 2) = (−4, 4), which is still 2 lots. The zero arrow never counts. A0 = λ0 for every λ, so it tells you nothing. A negative λ flips an arrow but keeps it on its line. The mirror [0 1; 1 0] shows this. It keeps (1, 1) as it is, so λ = 1. It turns (1, −1) into (−1, 1), so λ = −1.

You can find them without hunting. Move everything to one side, so Av = λv becomes Av − λv = 0. You cannot take a number from a matrix. So write λv as λIv. Here I is the matrix that leaves every arrow alone. Then (A − λI)v = 0. So v is a nonzero arrow that A − λI crushes to zero. It lies in the null space of A − λI. A square matrix crushes a nonzero arrow only when it flattens. A flat result has area scale 0, or volume scale 0 in space. So the eigenvalues are the values of λ that make det(A − λI) = 0.[^2] This is the [[characteristic equation]]. For our A, A − λI = [3 − λ 1; 0 2 − λ]. Its determinant is (3 − λ)(2 − λ). That is 0 at λ = 3 and λ = 2.

For any 2 by 2 matrix [a b; c d], det(A − λI) = (a − λ)(d − λ) − bc. Multiplied out, that is λ² − (a + d)λ + (ad − bc). The sum of the diagonal, a + d, is the [[trace]]. The number term, ad − bc, is the determinant. Say the two roots are p and q. Then the same quadratic is (λ − p)(λ − q) = λ² − (p + q)λ + pq. Matching the two, the eigenvalues add up to the trace.[^3] They multiply to the determinant. Take B = [2 −1; −1 2]. Its trace is 4 and its determinant 3. So λ² − 4λ + 3 = 0, and λ = 1 or 3.

To find each direction, put each λ back. For λ = 1, B − I = [1 −1; −1 1]. Both rows say v₁ − v₂ = 0. So v = (1, 1), or any multiple. For λ = 3, B − 3I = [−1 −1; −1 −1]. That gives v₁ + v₂ = 0, so v = (1, −1). One nonzero row is enough in a 2 by 2. A zero determinant means one row is a multiple of the other. Check: B(1, −1) = (2 + 1, −1 − 2) = (3, −3). That is 3 lots of (1, −1).

Some matrices have fewer lines. The quarter turn [0 −1; 1 0] turns every arrow through 90°. So Av is always square to v and never on its line. Its equation is λ² + 1 = 0, so λ = ±j. In a 2 by 2, complex roots mean no real line stays put. The shear [1 1; 0 1] gives (1 − λ)² = 0, so λ = 1 twice. Yet it has only one line. A − I = [0 1; 0 0] crushes just the line through (1, 0). A 3 by 3 matrix works the same way, with a cubic in place of the quadratic.

Eigenvalues earn their keep wherever two things are coupled. For two masses joined by springs, (1, 1) and (−1, 1) are the eigenvectors. Each one is a natural way to swing: together, or opposite.[^4] Coupled tanks and coupled circuits work the same way.

**An eigenvector is a nonzero arrow that a matrix keeps on its own line, Av = λv, and its eigenvalue λ is a root of det(A − λI) = 0.**[^2]

analogy.text: A common-mode choke has two equal windings on one core. Each winding has self-inductance L. Each links the other by mutual inductance M. So the pair acts like the matrix [L M; M L] on how fast the two currents change. Count each current positive the way that adds flux. Equal currents, (1, 1), add in the core and see L + M. Line out and neutral back, (1, −1), cancel in the core and see L − M. Those are the choke's two eigenvectors. L + M and L − M are their eigenvalues. Any other pair of currents splits into those two parts. Each part sees its own inductance.
analogy.breaks: Real windings are not exactly equal. So the two directions sit a little off (1, 1) and (1, −1). The matrix turns how fast the currents change into voltages, through voltage = L × di/dt. It does not turn the currents themselves into voltages. The choke's matrix is also symmetric, so its two directions are square to each other. A's directions are not. (1, 0) and (−1, 1) meet at 135°.

practice.text:
- Write A − λI by taking λ off each diagonal entry.
- Set its determinant to 0. For a 2 by 2 [a b; c d], that is λ² − (a + d)λ + (ad − bc) = 0.
- Solve for λ. Check that the roots add up to the trace and multiply to the determinant.
- For each λ, solve (A − λI)v = 0. In a 2 by 2, one nonzero row is enough. The other is a multiple of it.
- Write each eigenvector beside its own λ. Any nonzero multiple of it is just as right.
- Check by multiplying. Av must come out as λ lots of v.

**Rules of thumb:** if every entry on one side of the diagonal is 0, the eigenvalues are the diagonal entries. A matrix [a b; b a] has (1, 1) with a + b, and (1, −1) with a − b. In a 2 by 2, complex roots mean no real line stays put. A quarter turn is the example. A root that comes twice may give only one line. The shear [1 1; 0 1] is the example.

**Worked example:** take C = [1 1 0; 1 2 1; 0 1 1]. Expand det(C − λI) along the top row. You get (1 − λ)[(2 − λ)(1 − λ) − 1] − 1 × (1 − λ). That is (1 − λ)[(2 − λ)(1 − λ) − 2] = (1 − λ)(λ² − 3λ) = λ(1 − λ)(λ − 3). So λ = 0, 1 or 3. They add to 4. The diagonal adds to 1 + 2 + 1 = 4 too. For λ = 0, the rows say v₁ + v₂ = 0 and v₂ + v₃ = 0. So v = (1, −1, 1). That line is C's null space. For λ = 1, C − I = [0 1 0; 1 1 1; 0 1 0]. So v₂ = 0 and v₁ + v₃ = 0, giving (1, 0, −1). For λ = 3, the top row of C − 3I says −2v₁ + v₂ = 0. The bottom row says v₂ − 2v₃ = 0. Together they give (1, 2, 1). Check: C(1, 2, 1) = (3, 6, 3). That is 3 lots of (1, 2, 1).

**Common mistakes**
- Writing A − λ for A − λI. You can only take a matrix from a matrix.
- Reading the eigenvalues off the diagonal when a 2 by 2 has entries above and below the diagonal. [5 2; 2 2] has eigenvalues 1 and 6, not 5 and 2.
- Giving v = 0. Every matrix crushes the zero arrow, so it never counts as an eigenvector. Getting it means a slip, often in λ.
- Thinking an eigenvector is one arrow. (1, 1) and (2, 2) are both eigenvectors, on one line.
- Swapping the pairs. Each eigenvector goes with the λ you put in to find it.
- Working out a second eigenvalue from scratch when you know one. In a 2 by 2, the trace minus the one you know gives the other.

checks.label: Each eigenvector has an eigenvalue, the factor by which it is stretched or squished: for every flat matrix on the page and each of its lit lines, Av is exactly λ lots of v, λ is Av’s length over v’s length, and λ is negative only when Av points the opposite way; the same holds for C’s three lines in space
Non-trivial solutions exist if det(A − λI) = 0: on both λ slider screens, at every λ from −2 to 6, a nonzero crushed line is drawn exactly when det(A − λI) = 0, and A − λI sends it to zero
The sum of the eigenvalues is the sum of the diagonal terms, the trace: for every matrix on the page with real eigenvalues, its eigenvalues add up to its diagonal, C’s three included

Every worked number is right: A(0, 1) = (1, 2), A(1, 0) = (3, 0), A(−1, 1) = (−2, 2), A(−2, 2) = (−4, 4), A(1, 1) = (4, 2); the mirror keeps (1, 1) and sends (1, −1) to (−1, 1); (3 − 2)(2 − 2) = 0; B has trace 4, determinant 3, eigenvalues 1 and 3, B − I = [1 −1; −1 1], B − 3I all −1, B(1, −1) = (3, −3); [4 1; 2 3] has trace 7, determinant 10, 5 along (1, 1) and 2 along (1, −2); A − 3I = [0 1; 0 −1] crushes (1, 0); C has trace 4, equation −λ³ + 4λ² − 3λ and C(1, 2, 1) = (3, 6, 3); [5 2; 2 2] has trace 7, determinant 6, 6 along (2, 1) and 1 along (1, −2); the shear has one line and the quarter turn none
Each puzzle’s answer comes from the rule, and each wrong answer offered is the slip its hint names
Each puzzle offers three different answers, accepts only the right one, and draws every wrong one in the warning colour
Before Check, no puzzle shows its answer; after a right answer, it does

Each demonstration passes and ends where the lesson says: v at (0, 1) with Av = (1, 2), then at (1, 0) with λ = 3, ending on the line through (−1, 1) with λ = 2; the mirror lighting (1, 1) with λ = 1, ending on (1, −1) with λ = −1; A − λI flat at λ = 2 crushing (−1, 1), at λ = 3 crushing (1, 0), ending at 2; B − λI flat at 1 crushing (1, 1), ending at 3 crushing (1, −1); B’s lines (1, 1) with 1 and (1, −1) with 3; C’s three lines with 0 (dashed), 1 and 3

While each demonstration plays, the rule holds at every moment: Av is always A times v; a line is lit only while Av lies along v’s line, with Av = λv; the grid drawn is always A − λI, and a crushed line appears only while its area scale is 0 and is sent to zero

The probe snaps onto a lit line within 3° and lights only there: for every matrix on the page at every half degree, the line lights exactly when v is within 3° of one, and then Av = λv; the quarter turn never lights, the shear lights one line and the mirror two
Every demonstration has finished arriving within its 3 to 5 s, none starting before the 0.35 s screen fade ends; every answer’s motion, right or wrong, within 2.5 s

applied.problem: The [^1] sentence drops the source's "or squished", and the bold rule's "only stretches" is false for λ = 0 (the worked example's (1, −1, 1) is crushed) and flips; "area scale 0" is wrong for the 3 by 3 case, where it is volume.

"Not on the currents themselves" is false: the same inductance matrix turns the currents into flux linkages. What is true is that it gives the voltages from the rates of change, not from the currents.
